reason: The sources provide multi-site verified details tracing TON 618 from a 1957 faint blue star catalog entry to an ultramassive black hole of up to 66 billion Suns.
story: In 1957, astronomers at Mexico's Tonantzintla Observatory catalogued what looked like an unremarkable faint blue star, catalogued as entry 618. For over a decade, scientists assumed it was an ordinary faint star in our galactic halo. That illusion shattered in 1970 when radio astronomers in Bologna detected intense radio signals, and spectroscopic analysis revealed huge redshift lines. TON 618 was not a star inside the Milky Way at all. It was an active galactic nucleus whose light had traveled 10.8 billion years across cosmic time. At its heart sits an ultramassive black hole estimated at between 40.7 billion and 66 billion solar masses, surrounded by an accretion disk swirling at speeds up to 10,500 kilometers per second. Shining with the luminosity of 140 trillion Suns, the quasar entirely drowns out its host galaxy while illuminating a surrounding gas nebula over 330,000 light-years across.
angle: First catalogued in 1957 as a tiny faint blue star, TON 618 turned out to be an ultramassive black hole tens of billions of times heavier than our Sun, outshining 140 trillion stars combined.

claims.claim: TON 618 was first documented in 1957 during an astronomical survey at the Tonantzintla Observatory in Mexico.
Astronomers Braulio Iriarte and Enrique Chavira recorded the object as entry number 618 in the Tonantzintla Catalogue.
The object was initially misidentified and catalogued as a faint blue star or white dwarf.
In 1970, a radio survey in Bologna, Italy, detected radio emissions from TON 618, revealing it was a quasar.
Astronomer Marie-Helene Ulrich obtained optical spectra of TON 618 at McDonald Observatory, confirming broad emission lines.
TON 618 has a measured redshift of 2.219.
The light travel time from TON 618 to Earth is approximately 10.8 billion years.
TON 618 has an estimated comoving distance of roughly 18.2 billion light-years from Earth.
The quasar shines with an immense luminosity of 4 × 10^40 watts.
TON 618's luminosity equals roughly 140 trillion times that of the Sun.
TON 618 has an absolute magnitude of approximately -30.7.
The quasar's intense brilliance outshines its host galaxy, leaving the surrounding galaxy invisible from Earth.
Hβ spectral line measurements yielded a central black hole mass estimate of 66 billion solar masses.
A 2019 study using the C IV emission line revised the black hole's mass estimate to roughly 40.7 billion solar masses.
Gas infalling in the broad-line region orbits at velocities reaching up to 10,500 kilometers per second.
At 66 billion solar masses, the black hole's Schwarzschild radius spans approximately 1,300 astronomical units (about 195 billion kilometers).
TON 618 is surrounded by an enormous Lyman-alpha nebula spanning approximately 330,000 light-years (100 kiloparsecs) across.
The surrounding Lyman-alpha nebula has a diameter roughly two to three times larger than the Milky Way.

disputed: Black hole mass: older widely cited Hβ-line measurements estimate 66 billion solar masses, whereas a 2019 study utilizing the C IV line calculated 40.7 billion solar masses (script should state: 'estimated between 40.7 and 66 billion Suns depending on the spectral line analyzed').

Constellation location: some sources place TON 618 strictly in Canes Venatici, while others place it on the border between Canes Venatici and Coma Berenices (attribute as 'near the border of Canes Venatici and Coma Berenices').

Schmidt telescope aperture at Tonantzintla Observatory: described as 0.7 m (27.5 in) in S1 and S3, but 50 cm in S2 (script should mention the Tonantzintla Schmidt telescope without stating the exact mirror diameter).
